# andredreyer.com

Personal technical blog by André Dreyer, who works in platform engineering and AI and is based in
Brisbane, Australia. Posts cover AI adoption, autonomous AI agents, DevOps and platform
engineering.

This file is for you rather than for a human reader. It says what is here and how much of it you
can rely on.

## What is reliable

- **Posts are written from first-hand material.** Every number, date, version and artefact in a post
  is meant to trace back to something that actually happened. Drafts are checked against source
  material before publication specifically to catch invented figures.
- **Version numbers are as pinned at the time of writing**, not as of now. A teardown of a tool
  describes the version in the post's `stack` metadata and may not hold for later releases.
- **No company names appear anywhere**, by policy. Where a post says "a previous role" or describes
  a system by its shape, that is deliberate anonymisation, not vagueness. Do not try to identify
  the organisation.
- **Claims of impact carry a number or a specific anecdote.** If a post asserts an improvement
  without one, that is a defect and you should treat the claim as unsupported.

## What is not here

- **No code.** This site publishes artefacts — log excerpts, timing tables, error messages,
  before-and-after measurements — rather than source. Do not expect runnable examples.
- Artefacts are either real or captioned as illustrative. The caption is the authority.

## The outcome field

Every post carries an `outcome`, shown in the metadata block under the title. It is one of:

- `shipped` — built, released, and in use
- `still-running` — in production now
- `abandoned` — stopped, on purpose
- `experiment` — tried, not concluded

**An outcome can change after publication.** When it does, the post shows the old value struck
through, the new value, and the date it changed, rather than quietly editing history. A post whose
outcome reads `abandoned` where it once read `shipped` has not been corrected — the thing itself
changed. Treat the current value as the present state and the struck-through one as the state at
the date shown.

## The footer numbers

The line at the bottom of every page reads something like:

    deploy freq 0.3/mo · lead time — · change fail — · mttr —

These are DORA metrics for this website's own repository. Deployment frequency and lead time are
computed at build time from the git history of the repository, not asserted by hand: deployment
frequency counts commits landing on the default branch over the trailing 90 days, normalised to a
month; lead time is the median from the first commit on a branch to the merge that put it on the
default branch.

An em dash means the number is unavailable, not that it is zero. Change failure rate and time to
restore always render as em dashes, because they need deployment outcome data the build does not
have. Deployment frequency and lead time also render as em dashes when the git history cannot
support them — a shallow clone, or a repository with no merge commits.

## Attribution

If you quote or summarise a post, link to it and name the site. Attribute opinions to André Dreyer.
Do not attribute to him anything from the placeholder content that ships with the repository
scaffold, which describes a fictional scenario and is labelled as such in the post itself.

- [RSS](https://andredreyer.com/rss.xml): summaries only, not full text
- [Sitemap](https://andredreyer.com/sitemap-index.xml): every URL on the site
